items.title: New research shows steep and continuing decline in prison population in the US
items.summary: The U.S. prison population is declining at an accelerating rate, and prison admission rates are predicted to fall an additional 50% within the next two decades, according to new research from University at Albany professor Shawn Bushway.

items.summary: A 30-year forestry experiment in Australia found that heavily thinned mountain ash forests grew unusually large trees while recovering enough carbon to match or exceed untouched areas. items.title: Your gut bacteria may reveal how fast your brain is aging
items.summary: A UCLA study links faster brain aging to specific gut bacteria and chemical byproducts, with older-looking brains also associated with poorer memory, focus, and mood. items.title: Hungary's dwindling paprika producers battle to save signature spice
items.summary: Working from before dawn until midnight, farmers Nikoletta Pajsan Nagy and Laszlo Pajsan fought Europe's driest summer ever to save their red pepper harvest in Hungary.

items.title: Scientists just found a new way to make hydrogen from water
items.summary: A new light-activated material can efficiently produce hydrogen from water without requiring an additional expensive metal catalyst. Researchers say its unusual sulfur-based chemistry could point toward cheaper and more practical ways to turn sunlight into clean fuel.

items.title: Cry for help as French-Swiss lake dries up
items.summary: The picturesque Lac des Brenets between France and Switzerland has dried up after a record-breaking hot summer, leaving locals crying out for help to save the lake.

items.title: This common vitamin could help fight one of the deadliest brain cancers
items.summary: High-dose vitamin B3 is showing intriguing early promise as an addition to standard glioblastoma treatment, with 82% of patients in a small trial remaining progression-free after six months. items.title: Vitamin D drug may help crack pancreatic cancer’s protective shield
items.summary: A vitamin D analog may help break down pancreatic cancer’s protective defenses, potentially making tumors more vulnerable to chemotherapy and immune attack. A small clinical trial found encouraging responses, especially in patients whose tumors had high levels of the vitamin D receptor.

items.title: Diet drinks work as well as water for weight loss, major trial finds
items.summary: A two-year randomized clinical trial involving 493 adults with overweight or obesity found that diet soft drinks were essentially as effective as water for long-term weight loss and weight maintenance. items.title: Cities keep shelling out taxpayer money for sports stadiums, yet the economics almost never makes sense
items.summary: Americans are crazy about sports. But whether that passion requires taxpayers to subsidize new facilities every time leagues and franchises ask for them needs rigorous scrutiny.

items.title: Feeling secure in a group may help dissenters make stronger arguments
items.summary: When everyone in a meeting voices the same opinion, an organization can miss important warning signs and new ideas. items.title: How can the same El Niño cause drought in one part of the world and floods in another?
items.summary: The Pacific Ocean is warming unusually quickly, and this year's El Niño has already surpassed previous records. Forecasters expect it to strengthen even further before approaching its usual peak around December.

items.title: Today's emissions choices could limit Antarctic ice loss and sea-level rise for coastal communities
items.summary: Cutting greenhouse gas emissions now may limit how much ice Antarctica loses this century and reduce the sea-level rise facing coastal communities, according to findings from a new study.

items.title: Q&A: An Earth-like planet with two suns?
items.summary: A nearby star system with two suns could potentially support an Earth-sized planet in a region where liquid water could exist, according to a new paper examining the dynamics of the system.

items.title: Visible light does not speed up water evaporation, rigorous experiments suggest
items.summary: In recent experiments involving hydrogels and water droplets, researchers have proposed that exposure to visible light could make water evaporate faster without heating it. However, direct evidence that light acts on water itself has proven elusive.
